issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-themed conversations are hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 51-year-old school principal; this trigger implies a combat-related context not represented anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
issues.explanation: Avoiding people involved in the event or who look similar fits interpersonal/assault/accident traumas better than life-threatening illness, where there are typically no 'other people involved' in that sense. It is not well supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'talking about the future' as a trigger is plausible, but 'alcohol smell' is hard to connect unless alcohol was part of treatment context; nothing else in the profile supports that association, making this trigger set clinically incoherent.

'People can't be trusted' is more typical of interpersonal trauma and is poorly anchored to a life-threatening illness trauma in the absence of any treatment-related betrayal, conflict, or mistrust themes elsewhere in the profile.

'Crying' is not a trauma cue but an affective response/behavior, so it is clinically incoherent as a trigger item relative to the other trigger items, which are concrete sensory reminders linked to life-threatening illness (alcohol smell, hospital/antiseptic smell).

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: A global mistrust appraisal is a poor fit for the rest of the profile and trauma type. In life-threatening illness, the other items center on altered self and self-reliance, while 'People can't be trusted' implies an interpersonal betrayal/threat theme that is not supported by the memory, trigger, or strategy items and does not align well with the otherwise weak/inactive Threat links.

Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was fifty-one when the diagnosis came through-stage three lymphoma, discovered during a routine physical he'd almost skipped. He remembered the oncologist's voice, the smell of that examination room, the way his hands had trembled as he signed consent forms for chemotherapy. He'd survived eighteen months of treatment: the port in his chest, the chemicals burning through his veins, the hospital smell that became the smell of his own mortality. His wife Sarah had held his hand through most of it. Two years after remission, she died in a car accident on a Tuesday afternoon. Marcus had been at work, principal of Lincoln Elementary, when the police called. He'd never made it to the hospital in time to say goodbye.

The first months after Sarah's death were numb. But by autumn, something had shifted. Walking past the hospital on his drive home from school, Marcus felt his chest tighten, his breathing shallow. The smell-that particular antiseptic tang that drifted through the parking lot-sent him spiraling. He couldn't name what he was afraid of anymore. The cancer was gone. Sarah was gone. But his body seemed to remember something his mind couldn't quite grasp, a sensation of paralysis and dread that arrived without warning whenever he caught that hospital smell or, worse, when someone mentioned needing blood work. The feeling came as pure terror, sometimes without any clear image-just the overwhelming sense that he was dying, that his body was betraying him again.

Marcus had come to believe that he could no longer trust himself. He'd survived cancer; he'd failed to reach Sarah in time. The person he'd been before-the steady principal, the man who made decisions, who led a school-felt like someone else entirely. Now, any unexpected demand triggered an elaborate defense: he began rehearsing conversations before meetings, scripting his words so carefully that colleagues noticed his stilted responses. When the school nurse mentioned scheduling a health screening, Marcus felt the familiar surge of panic, and he simply didn't show up. He began avoiding the hospital entirely, taking longer routes home, refusing to drive past it. The avoidance made him feel safer momentarily, but it also deepened his conviction that something was fundamentally wrong with him. He was weak. He couldn't rely on his own judgment anymore.

By spring, Marcus had begun isolating. Invitations from friends went unanswered. He'd rehearse reasons to decline dinner, practice the exact words he'd use to keep people at arm's length. His sister called repeatedly; he let the calls go to voicemail. The isolation fed his sense of being unreliable-if he couldn't show up for the people who cared about him, what kind of man was he? Meanwhile, whenever his mind drifted toward those eighteen months of treatment, or toward the day Sarah died, the memories came fragmented and strange. He'd feel his body hunching forward, the way he had in the chemo chair, without any accompanying image. Other times, the full weight of the hospital room would crash over him-the smell, the cold metal of the examination table, the certainty that he was going to die-yet when he tried to deliberately recall what had actually happened, the details scattered. He couldn't hold the narrative together.

The triggers accumulated. A colleague mentioned needing a colonoscopy, and Marcus felt his shoulders lock, his breath catch. The smell of hand sanitizer in the staff bathroom sent him out of the building. A student's parent came to his office smelling faintly of alcohol-perhaps from the night before-and Marcus's hands shook so badly he had to grip the desk. He wasn't sure why that particular smell terrified him; perhaps it was bound up with hospital waiting rooms, with the helplessness of watching others fall apart. Each trigger seemed to confirm what he'd already decided: that his body was unreliable, that he couldn't trust himself to manage even the simplest interaction. So he rehearsed more, avoided more, isolated further.

Marcus finally called a therapist in June, after his superintendent expressed concern about his increasingly withdrawn behavior and erratic attendance at administrative meetings. He sat in the waiting room of the clinic-a place that, mercifully, smelled like coffee and old carpet, not antiseptic-and told the therapist that he didn't know who he was anymore. He was terrified that he'd never work through this, that the person he'd been was gone for good. What he wanted most was to feel like himself again, to trust his body and his mind. What frightened him most was that he'd already tried so hard to protect himself through isolation and control, and it had only made him feel more alone.
